terms.gloss: cook until it is quite soft
terms.grammar: dōnec with the subjunctive, or the future indicative as in Cato
evidence: Cato Agr. 156: coquitō ūsque dōnec conmadēbit bene
terms.comment: Cato’s words for cabbage boiled soft; his edition spells the verb conmadēre, and Lewis & Short cites it from this passage alone. The plain verb is madēre (next term), and coquere dōnec madeat says the same in commoner words.

terms.gloss: be boiled soft, be done (of food)
evidence: Plaut. Men. 326: jam ergō haec madēbunt, faxō
Plaut. Pers. 92: collȳrae facite ut madeant et colȳphia
Verg. G. 1.196: quamvīs ignī exiguō properāta madērent
terms.comment: To be wet, and so in the kitchen to be boiled soft (Lewis & Short): the cook’s promise in Plautus, and Vergil’s beans, soft even over a small fire. See “wet”.

terms.gloss: colour, brown; in the passive, turn brown, go golden
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.60: cum in sōle ambulem, nātūrā fit ut colōrer (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Classically of skin browned by the sun. Used of food going golden in the pan it is ours: frīgere dōnec colōrētur; we have found no set phrase for it.

phrases.latin: Jam ergō haec madēbunt, faxō; nīl morābitur.
phrases.english: I’ll have these cooked soft in no time; there’ll be no delay.

phrases.latin: Collȳrae facite ut madeant et colȳphia, nē mihi incocta dētis.
phrases.english: See that the noodles and the meat are cooked soft; don’t serve me anything underdone.

phrases.latin: grandior ut fētus siliquīs fallācibus esset, et quamvīs ignī exiguō properāta madērent
phrases.english: so that the yield in the deceptive pods might be bigger, and they might cook soft quickly, even over a small fire

phrases.latin: Coque dōnec madeant; tum aquam dēfunde.
phrases.english: Cook them until they’re soft; then pour off the water.

sources: Lewis & Short: commadeo · Lewis & Short: madeo · Lewis & Short: coloro
